title: Spain Train Crash Toll Rises to 69 as Rescuers Search Mangled Carriages
excerpt: A Renfe train authorised to proceed after a signal failure hit a stationary Iryo train near Urda, Toledo, in Spain's second fatal high-speed crash this year; 57 people remain in hospital and three days of national mourning have been declared.
body:
• Spain's official death toll from Wednesday's high-speed train collision near Urda, in Toledo province, rose to 69 on Thursday, with 57 injured people still in hospital.
  • A state-run Renfe train was authorised to proceed at normal speed after a signal failure, even though a stationary Iryo train was ahead of it on the Madrid-Seville line, Transport Minister Oscar Puente said.
  • More than 800 military and police personnel, over 200 vehicles, three helicopters and search dogs were deployed as cranes lifted wreckage through the night.
  • Spain has declared three days of national mourning for its second fatal high-speed rail crash this year, and campaigning for the November 29 snap election has been suspended.

Rescuers picked through mangled carriages on Thursday in a search for victims of Spain's second fatal high-speed train crash this year, with the death toll rising to 69 and the public demanding explanations for the latest accident, according to Reuters. Cranes had worked through the night to lift parts of the wreckage of Wednesday's crash near Urda, in the central Spanish province of Toledo, while emergency workers removed what appeared to be a body wrapped in a blanket from one of the trains.

Regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said the number of deaths had risen to 69 and that human remains had been found during rescue efforts, which now involved crane operations, particularly on a carriage that remained overturned. Authorities said 57 of those injured remained in hospital. Among those killed was Fatima Banez, a former labour minister who chaired the social and corporate responsibility arm of Spain's employers' association. Spain's Foreign Ministry said 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, of whom one was killed and at least seven injured.

How the collision happened

The crash happened after several trains stopped due to a signal failure. A Renfe train was then authorised to proceed at normal speed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, Puente said on Wednesday. The government has said that the decision to authorise the Renfe train to continue its journey was "inexplicable". The collision occurred at around 09:00 local time on Wednesday, when a high-speed train struck a stationary train carrying, in total, more than 500 passengers, according to AnewZ, which also reported survivors describing how they smashed windows to escape.

Puente rejected criticism that the system was unsafe, calling it "reliable and safe". A judge in Toledo sealed the crash site with a 2-kilometre exclusion zone along the Madrid-Seville line to preserve evidence.

A provisional toll, and a disputed figure

All casualty figures in this disaster remain provisional while recovery and identification work continues. Some Spanish media and RTVE were reported to have put a provisional toll as high as 74 on Thursday, a figure the rail accident investigation body briefly showed before the official count was kept at 69. Readers should treat 69 as the official toll confirmed by the regional government and Reuters, and expect it to change only if authorities confirm further deaths.

Unions blame lack of funding

The accident has added urgency to a debate about safety on Spain's railways, Europe's longest high-speed network and until recently a source of national pride. Train drivers went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety.

"We will continue demanding the necessary measures to make this sector safe again. It must have all the safety systems required to maintain the quality standards we have always had."

— Diego Martin, train drivers' union SEMAF

"We cannot tolerate, under any circumstances, this type of incident happening again," Martin said at Madrid's Atocha railway station. Unions blamed a lack of funding and will to improve safety, saying talks after January's crash were abandoned by the government in April. Renfe, the state-run rail operator, said the strike caused significant disruption and passengers could change or cancel tickets free of charge.

Mourning and political fallout

Spain has declared three days of national mourning, and Pope Leo sent condolences to the families of those killed. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who travelled to Toledo, said authorities were working "day and night" to support victims and to "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".

The crash followed another fatal accident in January involving the same rail companies on the same line, and has upended campaigning for the November 29 snap election, with both main party leaders suspending events. It is Europe's deadliest train accident since the Santiago de Compostela derailment in 2013.

What happens next

Investigators must establish why the Renfe train was authorised to proceed, examining the signalling failure, control-centre decisions and train data before any final cause is announced. The Madrid-Seville line remains disrupted around the sealed site.
